rationale: A wins because it turns the missing facts into the story instead of decorating around them. Its strongest line, "On's recycled-shoe pledge meets the question it won't answer: how much actually gets remade?" is clean pressure. B has useful shape, but "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" smuggles in an unsupported premise, and that is how pitches get killed in fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "a core product" is not supported. The update says Cyclon is On's recyclable running shoe, not that it is core to the business.
The next step says the category angle is "the most defensible," but the contrarian recycling-rate angle is sharper from the facts provided.
"ownership-to-access shift in physical retail" is plausible, but it needs outside evidence before it becomes more than a tidy frame.
gaps_in_B: "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" is invented from outside the update. Useful if sourced, fatal if pitched as given.
"The castor-bean sourcing implies a non-petroleum base and a specific supply chain" overreaches. Castor-bean-based material is in the update; the supply-chain implication is not.
"return rates are not disclosed" gets muddled with the actual fact: recycling-rate and per-unit economics are not disclosed. Return rate may matter, but it was not stated.
"Running Shoes Made From Castor Beans" risks novelty-product coverage unless On can provide technical specs or third-party verification.
